content: A set is a collection of distinct objects that are considered as a single entity. Sets are one of the most fundamental concepts in mathematics, and the study of their structure, known as set theory, is a rich and ongoing field of research. Although set theory was only developed at the end of the 19th century, it has become a cornerstone of modern mathematics and is introduced in primary education in many countries. Set theory serves as a foundational framework from which nearly all of mathematics can be derived. Philosophically, sets are often regarded as abstract objects. For example, three cups on a table, when referred to collectively as the cups, can be considered a set. Similarly, the symbols enclosed by curly brackets on a chalkboard represent a set. However, some proponents of mathematical realism, such as Penelope Maddy, argue that sets are concrete objects. Georg Cantor, the founder of set theory, defined a set as a collection of definite, distinct objects, which are called the elements or members of the set. These elements can be anything, such as numbers, people, letters, or even other sets. Sets are typically denoted by capital letters. Two sets are considered equal if and only if they have exactly the same members. Unlike multisets, sets do not allow duplicate elements, and the order of elements in a set is irrelevant. There are two primary ways to describe a set. The first is by an intensional definition, which uses a rule or description to specify the elements. The second is by an extensional definition, which explicitly lists all the elements of the set, enclosed in curly braces. In an extensional definition, the order of elements and repetitions are irrelevant. For example, the set {1, 2, 3} is equivalent to {3, 2, 1} or {1, 1, 2, 3}. For large or infinite sets, ellipses (...) are often used to indicate continuation. For instance, the set of positive even numbers can be written as {2, 4, 6, 8, ...}. Set-builder notation is another way to describe sets, where a rule is used to define the elements. For example, the set of integers that are four less than perfect squares can be written as {n² − 4 : n is a whole number}. Membership in a set is denoted by the symbol ∈, while non-membership is denoted by ∉. For example, if A is a set, 4 ∈ A means that 4 is an element of A, while 9 ∉ A means that 9 is not an element of A. The cardinality of a set, denoted |S|, refers to the number of elements in the set. For example, the set of colors in the French flag has a cardinality of 3. A set with no elements is called the empty set, denoted by ø, and its cardinality is 0. The empty set is a fundamental concept in mathematics and is a subset of every set. Some sets have infinite cardinality, such as the set of natural numbers (N). Interestingly, not all infinite sets have the same cardinality; for example, the set of real numbers (R) has a greater cardinality than the set of natural numbers. A subset is a set whose elements are all contained within another set. If A is a subset of B, this is written as A ⊆ B. If A is a subset of B but not equal to B, it is called a proper subset, denoted A ⊂ B. The empty set is a subset of every set, and every set is a subset of itself. The power set of a set S, denoted 2^S, is the set of all subsets of S, including the empty set and S itself. If S has n elements, its power set has 2^n elements. Certain sets are so commonly used in mathematics that they have special names and notations. For example: ℙ represents the set of all prime numbers. ℕ represents the set of natural numbers {1, 2, 3, ...}. ℤ represents the set of integers {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...}. ℚ represents the set of rational numbers, which includes all fractions. ℝ represents the set of real numbers, including both rational and irrational numbers. ℂ represents the set of complex numbers. Basic operations on sets include unions, intersections, complements, and Cartesian products. The union of two sets A and B, denoted A ∪ B, is the set of all elements that are in either A or B. The intersection of A and B, denoted A ∩ B, is the set of all elements that are in both A and B. If A and B have no elements in common, they are said to be disjoint. The complement of a set A, denoted A′, consists of all elements not in A, relative to a universal set U. The Cartesian product of two sets A and B, denoted A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Set theory is foundational to mathematics and is used to define structures such as groups, fields, and rings in abstract algebra. Relations, which are subsets of Cartesian products, are another important application of set theory. For example, the set of ordered pairs (x, x²) defines the function f(x) = x². Naive set theory, which defines a set as any well-defined collection, initially sufficed for mathematical purposes. However, it led to paradoxes such as Russell's paradox and Cantor's paradox, which revealed inconsistencies in the naive definition. To address these issues, set theory was formalized using axioms based on first-order logic, giving rise to axiomatic set theory. Despite these developments, naive set theory remains useful for many practical purposes.
